## Start with a policy evaluation: did a training programme raise earnings?

A government funds job training for disadvantaged workers. Participants later
earn more than some nonparticipants. **How much of that difference was caused by
the programme?** Selection into treatment and treatment effectiveness are distinct questions.

Write $Y_i(1)$ for earnings with training and $Y_i(0)$ for earnings without it.
Only one is observed: $Y_i=D_iY_i(1)+(1-D_i)Y_i(0)$.
This first equation is bookkeeping for the missing counterfactual, not a
statistical distribution. We need an assignment design or assumptions before
regression can answer a causal question.

Consider illustrative workers in two equally sized prior-earnings groups.
Treated and control outcome means are 14 and 12 thousand dollars in the first
group, and 24 and 20 in the second. The equally weighted adjusted contrast is
$\tfrac12(14-12)+\tfrac12(24-20)=3$ thousand dollars.
If treated workers are disproportionately in the higher-earnings group, an
unadjusted difference uses different weights and need not equal 3.

BART replaces these two coarse groups with a flexible conditional-mean surface
$f(d,x)$. Under consistency, overlap and conditional exchangeability,
$E[Y(d)\mid X=x]=f(d,x)$. For each posterior surface draw calculate

$$\tau^{(s)}=\frac1n\sum_i[f^{(s)}(1,x_i)-f^{(s)}(0,x_i)].$$

If three illustrative draws give effects 2, 3 and 4, their average is 3, but
the spread is essential: it records uncertainty about the fitted causal mean
contrast. Three draws are only an explanation, not an adequate MCMC run.
Both treatment predictions must use the same surface draw.

The empirical application uses a job-training policy setting, while the
simulation exercise lets us check recovery against a known effect. Randomised
and observational comparison samples support different identifying assumptions.
If important confounders are unobserved, flexibility alone does not fix the
problem; the later IV section asks what additional information an instrument supplies.

## From prediction to causation

Almost everything so far has treated estimation as learning a distribution that describes the data
well. A causal question is different in kind. We do not want to know what a treated firm looks like;
we want to know what that same firm would have looked like had it not been treated. That comparison
is never observed for any single unit, which is why causal inference is often called a missing-data
problem wearing econometric clothing. Once the causal effect is an unknown parameter, a posterior
gives a whole distribution over it, conditional on the causal identification assumptions and the statistical model. Identification assumptions are additional restrictions; they are not established by a good likelihood fit.

Two obstacles recur in applied work and this lecture takes them in turn. The first is
**confounding**: units select into treatment on characteristics that also drive the outcome, so the
raw treated-minus-control contrast mixes the policy effect with composition. Conditioning on those
characteristics turns the causal problem into a regression problem, which makes the flexibility of
that regression the binding constraint. The second is **endogeneity** of a continuous policy
variable, determined jointly with the outcome, where conditioning cannot help and we need an
instrument that shifts the policy without touching the outcome.

The Bayesian answers share a shape. For endogeneity we write a small simultaneous system and sample
its posterior with a Gibbs sampler, so the error correlation that breaks least squares becomes just
another parameter with a posterior. For confounding we make the conditional mean flexible enough
that no curvature is left to be blamed on the treatment, for which Bayesian additive regression
trees after Chipman, George and McCulloch (2010) and Hill (2011) are the standard tool.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})
```

## Specify the comparison before writing a regression

Consider a training subsidy and a firm's subsequent employment. For one particular firm,
$Y_i(1)$ means employment if it receives the subsidy; $Y_i(0)$ means employment if the
same firm does not. These are two possible outcomes for the same unit, not the observed
outcomes of two different firms. Their difference defines the causal effect.

Why write the observed outcome as $D_iY_i(1)+(1-D_i)Y_i(0)$? Substitute the two possible
values of the treatment indicator. For $D_i=1$, the expression selects $Y_i(1)$; for
$D_i=0$, it selects $Y_i(0)$. This equation records which potential outcome is observed.
It does not yet tell us how to infer the missing one.

Comparing a treated firm with an untreated firm fills in that missing comparison only
under further assumptions. Suppose larger firms both seek subsidies and hire more people
without them. Their higher employment cannot all be attributed to the subsidy.
Conditioning on size compares firms with the same observed size, but is sufficient only
if no remaining unmeasured factor confounds treatment and employment.

The adjustment formula below therefore has three separate reasons: average within
covariate groups; use conditional exchangeability to compare treatment arms within a
group; use consistency to connect the potential outcome to the recorded outcome.
Overlap ensures that the relevant comparisons exist in the data. A flexible BART
regression helps estimate those within-group means. Bayes' theorem supplies uncertainty
conditional on the assumptions; it cannot turn an unjustified comparison into an
identified causal effect. We keep the causal assumptions separate from the distributional
assumptions that make the posterior computable.

## Potential outcomes and the treatment effect

Fix a binary treatment $D_i \in \{0, 1\}$. For each unit there are two potential outcomes, $Y_i(1)$
if treated and $Y_i(0)$ if not, with unit-level effect $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. Only one arm is
ever realised, $Y_i = D_i Y_i(1) + (1 - D_i) Y_i(0)$, so $\tau_i$ is unavailable for any single unit
and we settle for the **average treatment effect** $\tau = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]$.

Comparing mean outcomes across arms is unbiased only under random assignment, and in observational
data it is not: firms that adopt a policy and countries that liberalise differ from those that do
not, so any variable $X$ driving both selection and outcome is a confounder. The assumption that
restores identification is **unconfoundedness**, $(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp D \mid X$, together with the
overlap condition $0 < \Pr(D = 1 \mid X) < 1$. The average effect then becomes the adjusted contrast
$\tau = \mathbb{E}_X[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid D = 1, X] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid D = 0, X]]$, as set out by Imbens
and Rubin (2015). Estimation is now the problem of getting $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid D, X]$ right: whatever
the model cannot represent is correlated with $D$ and is charged to the treatment.

### Derive what the data identify

Consistency means $Y=Y(D)$ for the treatment as specified, including the assumed
absence of interference. For $d=0,1$, iterated expectation, unconfoundedness,
and consistency give

$$
\mathbb E[Y(d)]=\mathbb E_X\{\mathbb E[Y(d)\mid X]\}
=\mathbb E_X\{\mathbb E[Y(d)\mid D=d,X]\}
=\mathbb E_X\{\mathbb E[Y\mid D=d,X]\}.
$$

Overlap ensures both treatment arms have support at the covariates over which
we average. Subtract the two expressions to obtain the adjustment formula.
A flexible regression estimates its ingredients; it cannot establish that
important confounders were measured. Weak overlap can leave a narrow model-based
interval driven largely by extrapolation and the prior.

For a posterior surface draw $f^{(s)}$, compute
$\tau^{(s)}=n^{-1}\sum_i[f^{(s)}(1,X_i)-f^{(s)}(0,X_i)]$.
Both predictions must come from the **same surface draw** so their dependence is
preserved. The quantity is an average conditional mean effect at the empirical
covariate distribution, not a recovered individual missing potential outcome.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation: the estimand as missing data, and where its posterior comes from

Collect for each unit the pair $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1))$ and define the finite-sample average effect
$$
\tau_{fs} \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\big].
$$
Split the sum according to which arm was realised. For a treated unit the observed outcome is $Y_i(1)$
and the missing one is $Y_i(0)$; for a control unit it is the other way round. Writing $Y_i^{mis}$ for
whichever arm was not realised,
$$
\tau_{fs} \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(2D_i - 1)\big(Y_i - Y_i^{mis}\big).
$$
Check the two cases: with $D_i = 1$ the factor $(2D_i-1)$ is $+1$ and the bracket is
$Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$; with $D_i = 0$ the factor is $-1$ and the bracket is $Y_i(0) - Y_i(1)$, whose
negative is again $Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)$. So the estimand is a known linear function of data we have and data
we do not have, and nothing else. This is the sense in which causal inference is a missing-data
problem: there is no unknown parameter in that display at all.

A Bayesian therefore needs the posterior predictive distribution of the missing arm,
$$
p\big(Y^{mis} \mid Y^{obs}, D, X\big) \;=\; \int p\big(Y^{mis} \mid \theta, D, X\big)\,
p\big(\theta \mid Y^{obs}, D, X\big)\, d\theta .
$$
The first factor is where the identifying assumptions enter. Consistency says the observed outcome is
the potential outcome for the arm actually taken, so the model fitted on the treated units describes
$Y(1)$ and the model fitted on the controls describes $Y(0)$. Unconfoundedness,
$(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp D \mid X$, says that the arm a unit happened to take carries no further
information about its potential outcomes once $X$ is held fixed, so
$p(Y_i^{mis} \mid \theta, D_i, X_i) = p\big(Y_i(1 - D_i) \mid \theta, X_i\big)$: the missing arm of
unit $i$ is predicted by the *opposite* arm's fitted conditional distribution evaluated at unit $i$'s
own covariates. Overlap guarantees that there were units in that opposite arm near $X_i$ from which
to learn it.

The algorithm follows immediately. For each posterior draw $\theta^{(s)}$, impute
$Y_i^{mis,(s)}$ from the opposite-arm predictive at $X_i$, then compute
$\tau_{fs}^{(s)} = n^{-1}\sum_i (2D_i-1)(Y_i - Y_i^{mis,(s)})$. Repeating over draws gives a posterior
for $\tau_{fs}$ directly, with no estimator and no standard-error formula anywhere.

Two estimands are easy to confuse here. If we replace each imputed $Y_i^{mis,(s)}$ by its conditional
mean $f^{(s)}(1-D_i, x_i)$ rather than drawing it, we obtain
$\tau^{(s)} = n^{-1}\sum_i[f^{(s)}(1,x_i) - f^{(s)}(0,x_i)]$, the average conditional mean contrast
used in the rest of this chapter. The difference between the two is exactly the averaged residual
noise: the imputation adds an independent $-(2D_i-1)\varepsilon_i^{mis}/n$ to each term, contributing
variance $\sigma^2/n$ to the posterior. In the simulation below, with $\sigma^2 = 1$ and $n = 600$,
that is a standard deviation of $1/\sqrt{600} = 0.041$, so the finite-sample estimand carries a
posterior noticeably wider than the conditional mean estimand even though both are called "the average
treatment effect". Report which one you computed.
:::

## A confounded policy experiment

The chunk below simulates a confounder that drives selection through a non-linear propensity and
also enters the outcome non-linearly, with a constant true effect of two.

**Reading the computation.** Selection depends on the same nonlinear covariate that drives outcomes. The naive contrast therefore combines treatment and composition; the simulation lets us see both parts.

```{python}
n, tau_true = 600, 2.0
X = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, size=n)                       # confounder
prop = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(0.8 * X**2 - 1.0)))       # non-linear propensity
D = rng.binomial(1, prop)
f_X = 1.5 * np.sin(1.5 * X) + 0.7 * X**2               # non-linear confounding
Y = 1.0 + tau_true * D + f_X + rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, size=n)
print(f"share treated {D.mean():.3f}   true ATE {tau_true:.3f}   "
      f"naive difference in means {Y[D == 1].mean() - Y[D == 0].mean():.3f}")
```

The naive contrast overstates the effect by roughly forty per cent. Both tails of $X$ are more
likely to be treated and both carry large values of $f(X)$, so the treated group is drawn
disproportionately from high-outcome regions of covariate space: treatment and outcome are linked
through the *curvature* of $f$.

Before adjusting anything, it is worth checking whether the comparison is even supportable, which
is what the **overlap** condition asks. The figure below plots the estimated propensity score
separately for treated and control units, reusing `prop` and `D` from the simulation above.

**Reading the computation.** The two histograms describe the same non-linear propensity function evaluated at the treated and the control sub-samples. Overlap holds where both histograms put mass, and fails where one of them is empty.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
bins = np.linspace(0, 1, 30)
ax.hist(prop[D == 0], bins=bins, alpha=0.6, density=True, label="control (D=0)")
ax.hist(prop[D == 1], bins=bins, alpha=0.6, density=True, label="treated (D=1)")
ax.set_xlabel("estimated propensity  P(D=1 | X)"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend()
ax.set_title("Overlap: propensity scores by treatment status")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"propensity range, control: [{prop[D == 0].min():.3f}, {prop[D == 0].max():.3f}]")
print(f"propensity range, treated: [{prop[D == 1].min():.3f}, {prop[D == 1].max():.3f}]")
```

Both groups occupy roughly the same range of propensity scores, with neither histogram empty where
the other has mass, so the overlap assumption is not obviously violated here, and a flexible model
has genuine treated-and-control pairs to compare at every covariate value. Overlap this good is a
property of the simulation; in applied work it is common to find regions with only treated or only
control units, where no amount of modelling can substitute for the missing comparison.

## Bayesian adjustment with a linear model

The natural first response is to add $X$ to the regression. With design matrix $Z$ collecting an
intercept, the treatment and the covariates, prior $\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau_0^2 I)$ and
likelihood $Y \mid \beta \sim \mathcal{N}(Z\beta, \sigma^2 I)$, the conjugate posterior of Lecture 2
applies unchanged: $\beta \mid Y \sim \mathcal{N}(m, V)$ with $V = (\sigma^{-2} Z^\top Z +
\tau_0^{-2} I)^{-1}$ and $m = \sigma^{-2} V Z^\top Y$, so the treatment coefficient has a univariate
Gaussian marginal read straight off $m$ and $V$. We compute it twice, ignoring the confounder and
then with a linear term in $X$.

**Reading the computation.** The adjustment model is Gaussian conditional on an estimated residual variance. Adding only a linear covariate cannot remove nonlinear confounding, however precise the coefficient posterior appears.

```{python}
def bayes_linreg(Z, y, sigma2=1.0, tau0=10.0):
    """Posterior mean and covariance of a conjugate Gaussian linear model."""
    V = np.linalg.inv(Z.T @ Z / sigma2 + np.eye(Z.shape[1]) / tau0**2)
    return V @ (Z.T @ y) / sigma2, V

one, Z_lin = np.ones(n), np.column_stack([np.ones(n), D, X])
s2_hat = np.var(Y - Z_lin @ np.linalg.lstsq(Z_lin, Y, rcond=None)[0], ddof=3)
m_raw, V_raw = bayes_linreg(np.column_stack([one, D]), Y, s2_hat)
m_lin, V_lin = bayes_linreg(Z_lin, Y, s2_hat)
post_raw = stats.norm(m_raw[1], np.sqrt(V_raw[1, 1]))
post_lin = stats.norm(m_lin[1], np.sqrt(V_lin[1, 1]))
for name, p in [("no adjustment", post_raw), ("linear in X", post_lin)]:
    print(f"{name:>14}: mean {p.mean():.3f}  95% CI "
          f"[{p.ppf(0.025):.3f}, {p.ppf(0.975):.3f}]")
```

Adjustment helps a little and nowhere near enough; both credible intervals sit well above two. The
reason is structural. The propensity depends on $X^2$ and is symmetric about zero, so treatment is
almost uncorrelated with $X$ itself and a linear term removes almost none of the relevant
confounding: a straight line cannot absorb curvature. The posterior is silent about this
misspecification: a narrow credible interval speaks about noise, not about whether the model is
right.

Seeing the raw comparison next to the two adjusted posteriors on one axis makes the point at a
glance. The figure below reuses `post_raw` and `post_lin` from the block above alongside the naive
difference in means.

**Reading the computation.** The dashed vertical line is a single number, the raw contrast; the two curves are full posteriors for the same quantity under two adjustment models. Distance from the dotted true-effect line is the remaining bias in each case.

```{python}
naive_diff = Y[D == 1].mean() - Y[D == 0].mean()
tgrid_lin = np.linspace(0.5, 3.5, 400)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.axvline(naive_diff, color="grey", ls="--", label=f"naive difference = {naive_diff:.2f}")
ax.plot(tgrid_lin, post_raw.pdf(tgrid_lin), label="no adjustment (posterior)")
ax.plot(tgrid_lin, post_lin.pdf(tgrid_lin), label="linear in X (posterior)")
ax.axvline(tau_true, color="black", ls=":", label=f"true ATE = {tau_true:.1f}")
ax.set_xlabel(r"treatment effect $\tau$"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
ax.set_title("Confounded comparison versus adjusted posteriors")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The raw comparison and the two posteriors are all bunched together, well to the right of the true
effect, and adding a linear term in $X$ shifts the density only slightly. None of these three numbers
comes close to the truth, which is the visual version of the "helps a little and nowhere near enough"
verdict above, and it motivates the flexible surface built later in the chapter.

## Bayesian instrumental variables

Confounding by observables is only one way a comparison fails. Suppose the policy variable is
continuous and determined jointly with the outcome. Write the **triangular simultaneous system**, a
first stage for the endogenous regressor $x_i$ and a structural equation for the outcome $y_i$,

$$
x_i = z_i^\top \gamma + v_i , \qquad
y_i = \beta\, x_i + w_i^\top \delta + u_i , \qquad
\begin{pmatrix} v_i \\ u_i \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left( 0, \;
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_v^2 & \sigma_{vu} \\ \sigma_{vu} & \sigma_u^2 \end{pmatrix}
\right) .
$$

The instruments $z_i$ enter the first stage but not the structural equation, which is the exclusion
restriction, and they must actually move $x_i$, which is relevance. The system is triangular, so the
map from $(v, u)$ to $(x, y)$ has unit Jacobian and the likelihood is just the bivariate normal
density of the two residuals.

Least squares fails as soon as $\sigma_{vu} \neq 0$. Since $x_i$ contains $v_i$, which is correlated
with the structural error, regressor and error are correlated, and the estimator converges to
$\beta + \operatorname{Cov}(x_i, u_i)/\operatorname{Var}(x_i)$, that is to
$\beta + \sigma_{vu} / (\gamma^\top \operatorname{Var}(z) \gamma + \sigma_v^2)$. The bias carries the
sign of $\sigma_{vu}$ and shrinks only as the instruments explain more of $x$. No prior repairs it,
because it is a property of the wrong likelihood; the fix is to model both equations at once.

To build a Gibbs sampler we factor the bivariate normal rather than stacking it. Conditional on
$\Sigma$, the regression of $u$ on $v$ has slope $\sigma_{vu} / \sigma_v^2$ and residual variance
$\sigma_u^2 (1 - \rho^2)$ with $\rho = \sigma_{vu} / (\sigma_v \sigma_u)$, which turns the
structural equation into a **control-function** form,

$$
y_i - \frac{\sigma_{vu}}{\sigma_v^2}\, v_i \;=\; \beta\, x_i + w_i^\top \delta + \eta_i ,
\qquad \eta_i \sim \mathcal{N}\!\big(0, \sigma_u^2 (1 - \rho^2)\big),
$$

in which the first-stage residual $v_i = x_i - z_i^\top \gamma$ is a known regressor and the
remaining error is independent of $x_i$. That is why the endogeneity disappears: once the part of
$u_i$ predictable from $v_i$ is subtracted, what is left is orthogonal to the regressor. Reversing
the roles gives the first-stage conditional, regressing $x_i - (\sigma_{vu} / \sigma_u^2) u_i$ on
$z_i$ with variance $\sigma_v^2 (1 - \rho^2)$. Both are ordinary Gaussian linear models, so with
Gaussian priors both draws are Gaussian.

The third block is the error covariance. With prior $\Sigma \sim \mathcal{IW}(\nu_0, S_0)$ and
residual matrix $E = [\,v \;\; u\,]$ of dimension $n \times 2$, conjugacy gives
$\Sigma \mid \gamma, \beta, \delta \sim \mathcal{IW}(\nu_0 + n, S_0 + E^\top E)$. We draw it
ourselves. If $W \sim \mathcal{W}(\nu, S^{-1})$ then $W^{-1} \sim \mathcal{IW}(\nu, S)$, and a
Wishart draw follows from the **Bartlett decomposition**: let $C$ be the Cholesky factor of $S^{-1}$
and $A$ be lower triangular with $A_{ii} = \sqrt{\chi^2_{\nu - i + 1}}$ and standard normals below
the diagonal, and set $W = (CA)(CA)^\top$. The chunk below implements both draws.

**Reading the computation.** Conditional Gaussian errors turn the IV block into an adjusted regression. The helper receives the adjusted design, outcome, variance, and prior precision so each update can be compared with its formula.

```{python}
def draw_gaussian(Xd, yd, s2, prec0, rng):
    """Draw from the Gaussian posterior of a linear model with known variance s2."""
    V = np.linalg.inv(Xd.T @ Xd / s2 + prec0)
    return V @ (Xd.T @ yd / s2) + np.linalg.cholesky(V) @ rng.standard_normal(Xd.shape[1])

def draw_inv_wishart(nu, S, rng):
    """Inverse-Wishart draw via a Bartlett-decomposed Wishart of the inverse."""
    A = np.zeros(S.shape)
    for i in range(S.shape[0]):
        A[i, i] = np.sqrt(rng.chisquare(nu - i))
        A[i, :i] = rng.standard_normal(i)
    CA = np.linalg.cholesky(np.linalg.inv(S)) @ A
    return np.linalg.inv(CA @ CA.T)

n_iv, beta_iv, alpha_iv, rho_iv = 500, 1.0, 0.5, 0.7
gamma_iv = np.array([0.3, 0.8])                    # first stage: intercept and slope
Zi = np.column_stack([np.ones(n_iv), rng.normal(size=n_iv)])
err = rng.standard_normal((n_iv, 2)) @ np.linalg.cholesky(
    np.array([[1.0, rho_iv], [rho_iv, 1.0]])).T
x_end = Zi @ gamma_iv + err[:, 0]
y_iv = alpha_iv + beta_iv * x_end + err[:, 1]
Xs = np.column_stack([x_end, np.ones(n_iv)])       # coefficients (beta, alpha)
b_ols = np.linalg.solve(Xs.T @ Xs, Xs.T @ y_iv)
res = y_iv - Xs @ b_ols
se_ols = np.sqrt((res @ res / (n_iv - 2)) * np.linalg.inv(Xs.T @ Xs)[0, 0])
print(f"true beta {beta_iv:.3f}   OLS beta {b_ols[0]:.3f}   95% interval "
      f"[{b_ols[0] - 1.96 * se_ols:.3f}, {b_ols[0] + 1.96 * se_ols:.3f}]")
```

The least-squares interval is tight and wrong, missing the truth by many multiples of its own
standard error, the signature of bias rather than imprecision. The sampler below cycles the three
blocks derived above under diffuse priors.

**Reading the computation.** After drawing the first-stage and structural coefficients, update their error covariance from current residuals. Correlation between the errors is the source of endogeneity, not a numerical defect to be removed by standardising.

```{python}
prec0, nu0, S0, n_draw, burn = np.eye(2) / 100.0, 4.0, np.eye(2), 6000, 2000
gamma = np.linalg.solve(Zi.T @ Zi, Zi.T @ x_end)
theta, Sigma = b_ols.copy(), np.eye(2)
th_draws, rho_draws = np.empty((n_draw, 2)), np.empty(n_draw)
for t in range(n_draw):
    sv2, su2, svu = Sigma[0, 0], Sigma[1, 1], Sigma[0, 1]
    rho = svu / np.sqrt(sv2 * su2)
    u = y_iv - Xs @ theta                          # structural residual
    gamma = draw_gaussian(Zi, x_end - (svu / su2) * u, sv2 * (1 - rho**2), prec0, rng)
    v = x_end - Zi @ gamma                         # first-stage residual
    theta = draw_gaussian(Xs, y_iv - (svu / sv2) * v, su2 * (1 - rho**2), prec0, rng)
    E = np.column_stack([x_end - Zi @ gamma, y_iv - Xs @ theta])
    Sigma = draw_inv_wishart(nu0 + n_iv, S0 + E.T @ E, rng)
    th_draws[t] = theta
    rho_draws[t] = Sigma[0, 1] / np.sqrt(Sigma[0, 0] * Sigma[1, 1])
beta_post, rho_post = th_draws[burn:, 0], rho_draws[burn:]
for nm, dr, tv in [("beta", beta_post, beta_iv), ("error corr", rho_post, rho_iv)]:
    lo, hi = np.quantile(dr, [0.025, 0.975])
    print(f"{nm:>11}: mean {dr.mean():.3f}   95% CI [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]   true {tv:.3f}")
```

The posterior for the structural coefficient is centred essentially on the truth and its credible
interval covers it, while the least-squares interval lies entirely above it. The sampler also
recovers the error correlation, the parameter that diagnoses the endogeneity in the first place: had
its posterior concentrated near zero we would have concluded that least squares was fine. The wider
Bayesian interval is the correct price of instrumenting, and it widens as the instrument weakens.

Two pictures make this concrete: the corrected posterior against the biased OLS estimate, and the
posterior of the correlation that caused the bias in the first place. Both reuse the `beta_post` and
`rho_post` draws already retained from the sampler.

**Reading the computation.** The dashed and dotted lines mark two single numbers, an estimate and the truth; the histogram is the full Bayesian IV posterior for the same coefficient.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(beta_post, bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.75, label="Bayesian IV posterior")
ax.axvline(b_ols[0], color="grey", ls="--", label=f"OLS = {b_ols[0]:.2f}")
ax.axvline(beta_iv, color="black", ls=":", label=f"true beta = {beta_iv:.1f}")
ax.set_xlabel(r"structural coefficient $\beta$"); ax.set_ylabel("posterior density")
ax.legend()
ax.set_title("Bayesian IV corrects the OLS endogeneity bias")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Reading the computation.** This histogram is a diagnostic, not the target of the analysis: a posterior for $\rho$ concentrated away from zero is what tells us least squares needed correcting at all.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(rho_post, bins=50, density=True, color="C2", alpha=0.8)
ax.axvline(rho_iv, color="black", ls=":", label=f"true corr = {rho_iv:.1f}")
ax.set_xlabel(r"error correlation $\rho$"); ax.set_ylabel("posterior density")
ax.legend()
ax.set_title("Posterior of the error correlation diagnoses the endogeneity")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The OLS line sits in the left tail of the Bayesian posterior, well outside where the corrected
estimate puts most of its mass, while the true value sits comfortably inside it. The correlation
posterior is concentrated well above zero and away from the true value of $\rho$ only by ordinary
sampling variation, which is exactly the signature that would have been absent had least squares
been valid to begin with.

### Interpret the IV conditionals before programming them

In the triangular system, conditional Normal algebra gives

$$
u_i\mid v_i,\Sigma\sim N\left(
\frac{\sigma_{vu}}{\sigma_v^2}v_i,
\sigma_u^2-\frac{\sigma_{vu}^2}{\sigma_v^2}\right).
$$

After subtracting the conditional error mean from $y_i$, the outcome equation
is a Gaussian regression with the smaller conditional variance. This is the
reason the Gibbs code constructs an adjusted outcome rather than simply
regressing on fitted values and treating them as observed without error.
The first-stage update uses the corresponding conditional distribution of $v_i$
given $u_i$. Neither update guarantees identification: exclusion, instrument
exogeneity, and relevance are substantive assumptions. With a weak instrument,
prior sensitivity is part of the result, not merely a numerical nuisance.

### The Normal update inside a tree

Fix all trees except one, subtract their predictions, and consider partial
residuals in a leaf: $r_i=\mu_\ell+\epsilon_i$, with
$\mu_\ell\sim N(0,s_\mu^2)$ and $\epsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$.
Completing the scalar square gives

$$
V_\ell=(s_\mu^{-2}+n_\ell/\sigma^2)^{-1},\qquad
m_\ell=V_\ell\sum_{i\in\ell}r_i/\sigma^2.
$$

The leaf conditional is $N(m_\ell,V_\ell)$. Small leaves receive stronger
shrinkage. BART additionally learns tree structures; keeping a fixed dictionary
of indicator functions gives a useful backfitting demonstration but a different
model. The exercise uses the tree model for the prescribed policy-effect task.

## A runnable stand-in for BART

Return to the confounding problem, where the failure was the rigidity of the adjustment. Bayesian
additive regression trees write the conditional mean as a sum of many shallow trees,
$\mathbb{E}[Y \mid D, X] = \sum_{m=1}^{M} g(D, X; T_m, \mu_m)$, under regularising priors that keep
every tree weak, with leaf values shrunk hard towards zero so that no single tree dominates.
The posterior is explored by **Bayesian backfitting**, updating each learner against the residual
left by all the others.

Sampling over tree topologies is more machinery than we want from scratch, so we simplify: keep the
logic, drop the search. It must be said plainly that what follows is a stand-in, not BART: the split
points are fixed in advance rather than learned, and the learners are stumps in one variable rather
than trees. What it shares with BART is the mechanism, many weak additive learners tied down by a
shrinkage prior and fitted by backfitting. We fix $M = 40$ cut-points on a coarse grid across the
confounder and make the $m$-th learner a constant stump,

$$
Y_i = \mu + \tau D_i + \sum_{m=1}^{M} a_m \mathbb{1}\{X_i > c_m\} + \varepsilon_i , \qquad
a_m \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(0, \; \frac{(0.8\, s_Y)^2}{M}\right), \qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) .
$$

The prior variance of each amplitude is divided by $M$, exactly as in BART's leaf prior, so the sum
keeps a sensible scale however many stumps we use while each is individually pulled towards doing
nothing. Every full conditional is standard: $a_m$ given the rest is a one-dimensional Gaussian,
$(\mu, \tau)$ given the ensemble is Gaussian, and $\sigma^2$ is inverse-Gamma.

**Reading the computation.** Backfitting adds one learner’s old contribution back to the residual, draws its new amplitude, and subtracts the new contribution. The cut points are fixed, so this illustrates an additive basis model rather than learned BART trees.

```{python}
M = 40
cuts = np.linspace(X.min(), X.max(), M + 2)[1:-1]
B = (X[:, None] > cuts[None, :]).astype(float)     # n x M stump basis
Bsq, Zc = (B * B).sum(0), np.column_stack([one, D])
sa2 = (0.8 * Y.std()) ** 2 / M                     # shrinkage prior on amplitudes
c0 = d0 = 0.01                                     # diffuse inverse-Gamma on sigma^2
n_bf, burn_bf = 4000, 1000
a, sigma2, g = np.zeros(M), Y.var(), np.zeros(n)
tau_draws, fit_draws = np.empty(n_bf), np.empty((n_bf, n))
for t in range(n_bf):
    theta_c = draw_gaussian(Zc, Y - g, sigma2, np.eye(2) / 100.0, rng)
    base = Y - Zc @ theta_c                        # Bayesian backfitting sweep
    r = base - g
    for m in range(M):
        r = r + a[m] * B[:, m]                     # add stump m back in
        prec = Bsq[m] / sigma2 + 1.0 / sa2
        a[m] = (B[:, m] @ r / sigma2) / prec + rng.standard_normal() / np.sqrt(prec)
        r = r - a[m] * B[:, m]                     # take the new stump out
    g = base - r
    e = Y - Zc @ theta_c - g
    sigma2 = 1.0 / rng.gamma(c0 + n / 2, 1.0 / (d0 + 0.5 * e @ e))
    tau_draws[t], fit_draws[t] = theta_c[1], theta_c[0] + g
tau_bf, fit_draws = tau_draws[burn_bf:], fit_draws[burn_bf:]
print(f"stump ensemble tau: mean {tau_bf.mean():.3f}   95% CI "
      f"[{np.quantile(tau_bf, 0.025):.3f}, {np.quantile(tau_bf, 0.975):.3f}]")
print(f"posterior sigma^2 {sigma2:.3f} (true 1.000)   true ATE {tau_true:.3f}")
```

The ensemble recovers the treatment effect. Where the linear adjustment left a bias of about three
quarters of a unit, the additive stumps put the posterior mean within a few hundredths of two and
the credible interval brackets it. The residual variance also lands near its true value of one,
direct evidence that the curvature in $X$ was absorbed by the learners rather than charged to the
treatment.

**Reading the computation.** The fitted surface and treatment posterior answer related questions: whether observable curvature is represented and what average treatment effect remains. Neither plot verifies the absence of unobserved confounding.

```{python}
order, fit_mean, tgrid = np.argsort(X), fit_draws.mean(0), np.linspace(1.6, 3.2, 400)
fit_lo, fit_hi = np.quantile(fit_draws, [0.025, 0.975], axis=0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
axes[0].plot(X[order], (1.0 + f_X)[order], "k", lw=1.8, label="true 1 + f(X)")
axes[0].plot(X[order], fit_mean[order], color="steelblue", lw=1.6, label="stump ensemble")
axes[0].fill_between(X[order], fit_lo[order], fit_hi[order], color="steelblue", alpha=0.3)
axes[0].set(xlabel="confounder X", ylabel="response", title="Learned adjustment surface")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=9)
axes[1].hist(tau_bf, bins=50, density=True, color="steelblue", alpha=0.85, label="stumps")
axes[1].plot(tgrid, post_lin.pdf(tgrid), color="darkorange", lw=1.8, label="linear in X")
axes[1].axvline(tau_true, color="black", ls=":", lw=1.6, label="true ATE = 2")
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"$\tau$", ylabel="posterior density", title="Bias removed by flexibility")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The left panel explains the right one. The ensemble traces the sine-plus-quadratic shape closely in
the middle of the covariate range and widens its band in the sparse tails, as a regularised fit
should. Nothing curved is left for $D$ to explain, and the wider credible interval is the price of
not assuming a functional form. Real BART learns where to split, handles many covariates and their
interactions, and lets the treatment interact with them, so that averaging the posterior contrast
$\hat{f}(1, X_i) - \hat{f}(0, X_i)$ over the sample gives an average effect even under heterogeneity.



## What tree flexibility learns, and what identifies the policy effect

The tree slides explain a prior for the outcome surface $f(d,x)$. To turn that
surface into a causal estimand requires a separate argument. Under consistency,
conditional exchangeability $(Y(0),Y(1))\perp D\mid X$, and overlap,

$$
E[Y(d)\mid X=x]=E[Y\mid D=d,X=x]=f(d,x).
$$

The first equality is justified by identification assumptions, not by a
flexible regression algorithm. For the observed covariate population, a posterior
draw of the average conditional treatment effect is therefore

$$
\tau^{(s)}=\frac1n\sum_i\{f^{(s)}(1,x_i)-f^{(s)}(0,x_i)\}.
$$

Stack both treatment assignments into one prediction matrix so that the same
sampled ensemble supplies both potential-outcome means. Independent fits or
independent prediction calls can lose their posterior dependence. Do not add
independent observation noise when the estimand is this average of conditional
means. Inferring a realised finite-sample average of individual potential-outcome
differences is another target and requires additional assumptions about those outcomes.

The exercise now fits actual BART trees. Compare the posterior effect plot with
the overlap plot: a smooth fitted surface cannot reveal unmeasured confounding,
and a narrow extrapolation interval does not establish overlap.

*Source connection:* SGPE Lecture 3, Part II, PDF pp. 4–19, supplies tree modelling;
Hill (2011) and Imbens and Rubin (2015) supply the causal interpretation.

## What these data can and cannot identify

Everything above ran on simulated data, and that was deliberate: a simulation is the only place where
the true effect is known and a method can be checked against it. The honest counterpart to that
convenience is to say plainly what happens when we turn to the data actually shipped with this course.
The repository holds macroeconomic series from FRED and portfolio returns from the Kenneth French
library. Neither contains a randomised experiment. Nobody assigned the federal funds rate at random,
nobody assigned an industry to the 2020 pandemic, and there is no lottery, no discontinuity and no
credible instrument sitting in these files waiting to be used. A chapter that produced a number and
called it a causal effect of monetary policy on equity prices would be teaching the wrong lesson.

What these data do support is two exercises that are worth doing carefully, provided their status is
stated. The first is an event study: pick a rule that says when a tightening cycle began, line the
market's return up in event time and ask what the posterior says about the average path around those
dates. The second is a synthetic-control style comparison: take one industry hit hard by a shock, build
a weighted combination of the other industries that tracked it before the shock, and look at the gap
afterwards. Both produce a posterior distribution over a well-defined quantity. In both cases that
quantity is a descriptive gap, not a treatment effect, and the rest of this section is about seeing
precisely how far that is from the causal quantity a policy maker would want.

The setup below loads the three files we need and reports what is in them.

**Reading the computation.** The funds rate and the market return are aligned on the same monthly index so that event time is unambiguous. The industry file is checked for the date from which all forty-nine portfolios are complete, because a synthetic control cannot use a donor that is missing.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())
rng_r = np.random.default_rng(2026)

fred_r = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "fred_macro_monthly.parquet")
ff_r = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_factors_monthly.parquet")
ind_r = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_industry49_monthly.parquet")

mkt = ff_r["mkt_rf"].reindex(fred_r.index).dropna()
print(f"funds rate: {fred_r.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {fred_r.index[-1]:%Y-%m}, "
      f"{len(fred_r)} months")
print(f"market excess return: {len(mkt)} matched months, mean {mkt.mean():.4f}, "
      f"sd {mkt.std(ddof=1):.4f}")
print(f"industry portfolios: {ind_r.shape[1]} series, complete from "
      f"{ind_r.dropna().index[0]:%Y-%m}")
```

The funds rate covers $800$ months from January 1960 to August 2026 and the market excess return
matches $799$ of them, averaging $0.0059$ per month with a standard deviation of $0.0445$. That ratio
is the background fact against which everything below has to be read: a monthly mean of about six tenths
of a percentage point sits inside a monthly standard deviation of four and a half percentage points, so
a year of data contains roughly $0.0059 \times 12 = 0.071$ of signal against
$0.0445\sqrt{12} = 0.154$ of noise. Any event-study effect we could hope to detect with a dozen episodes
must be large indeed. The forty-nine industry portfolios are complete from July 1969 onwards, which
fixes the earliest usable start for the second exercise.

## A Bayesian event study around Federal Reserve tightening cycles

### Writing the rule down in code

There is no official list of tightening episodes in these files, so we have to manufacture one, and the
manufacturing is the interesting part. A reasonable rule says that a tightening cycle has begun in month
$t$ if the federal funds rate is at least $\theta$ percentage points higher than it was twelve months
earlier, and if no episode has already been dated within the preceding $q$ months. The two numbers
$\theta$ and $q$ are choices, not facts. A low $\theta$ catches mild adjustments alongside genuine
cycles; a high $\theta$ keeps only the dramatic ones. A short $q$ splits a long tightening into several
episodes; a long $q$ merges neighbouring ones and, because the rule keeps the first qualifying month, it
also changes *which* month is called the start.

**Reading the computation.** The function returns event dates, not a regression. Everything downstream conditions on this list, so the list is the first place to look when an event-study result seems fragile.

```{python}
def tightening_starts(rate, window=12, threshold=1.5, quiet=24):
    """First month whose `window`-month rise in the policy rate reaches
    `threshold`, ignoring any such month within `quiet` months of the last start."""
    hot = rate.diff(window) >= threshold
    starts, last = [], None
    for date, is_hot in hot.items():
        if not is_hot:
            continue
        if last is not None and (date - last).days < quiet * 30.5:
            continue
        starts.append(date)
        last = date
    return pd.DatetimeIndex(starts)

starts_base = tightening_starts(fred_r["fed_funds"], 12, 1.5, 24)
starts_loose = tightening_starts(fred_r["fed_funds"], 12, 1.0, 18)
print(f"baseline rule (12-month rise >= 1.5pp, 24-month gap): {len(starts_base)} episodes")
print("  " + ", ".join(f"{d:%Y-%m}" for d in starts_base))
print(f"looser rule (>= 1.0pp, 18-month gap): {len(starts_loose)} episodes")
print("  " + ", ".join(f"{d:%Y-%m}" for d in starts_loose))
```

The baseline rule returns twelve episodes, and the list is recognisable as monetary history, among them
November 1966, January 1973, November 1977, December 1979 at the start of the Volcker disinflation,
November 1988, September 1994, May 2000, March 2005 and July 2022. The looser rule returns nineteen. Of
those, seven are episodes the baseline rule never dates at all, namely November 1969, July 1974,
November 1980, September 1987, July 2006, October 2018 and January 2024, and most of the remaining
twelve are shifted a few months earlier because the lower threshold is crossed sooner, so that the
2005 episode becomes December 2004 and the 2022 episode becomes June 2022. Seven extra episodes and a
dozen moved dates from changing two numbers that nobody can pin down from theory is the whole
methodological problem of this literature in one table.

**Reading the computation.** The vertical lines mark the dates the two rules produced. Where a solid and a dotted line nearly coincide the two rules agree; where a dotted line stands alone the looser rule has added an episode.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(fred_r.index, fred_r["fed_funds"], color="0.35", lw=1.0,
        label="federal funds rate")
for d in starts_base:
    ax.axvline(d, color="firebrick", lw=1.0, alpha=0.8)
for d in starts_loose:
    ax.axvline(d, color="steelblue", lw=0.8, ls=":", alpha=0.9)
ax.plot([], [], color="firebrick", lw=1.0, label="baseline rule start")
ax.plot([], [], color="steelblue", lw=0.8, ls=":", label="looser rule start")
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("per cent")
ax.set_title("Tightening episodes identified by two mechanical rules")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The plot makes the mechanics visible. Both rules fire densely through the volatile 1970s, when the
funds rate moved by whole percentage points within a year routinely, and sparsely after 1995, when it
moved more slowly and in pre-announced steps. That is itself a warning: an event study that pools these
dates is averaging across two very different monetary regimes, and the pre-1985 episodes will dominate
simply because there are more of them.

### The event-time posterior

Line each episode up at event month zero and collect the market's abnormal return, defined as the excess
return minus its full-sample mean, for event months $-12$ to $+24$. Stacking the episodes gives a matrix
with one row per episode and one column per event month, and the model is the simplest one that fits the
question: in event month $h$ the abnormal return of episode $k$ is
$$
r_{k,h} \;=\; \mu_h + \varepsilon_{k,h}, \qquad \varepsilon_{k,h} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2),
$$
with the conjugate pair $\mu_h \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 B_0)$ independently across
event months and $\sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{IG}(\alpha_0, \delta_0)$. This is a difference in means with
the comparison group folded into the definition of the outcome, so the algebra of the next callout
applies directly and there is nothing to sample: the posterior is available in closed form and we draw
from it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation: the posterior for a difference in means, and why the sharp null is a different object

Take two arms, $n_1$ treated observations with mean $\bar y_1$ and $n_0$ controls with mean $\bar y_0$,
and a Normal likelihood $y_i \mid D_i = d \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_d, \sigma^2)$. Use the course's
conjugate prior, $\mu_d \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 B_0)$ independently in each arm and
$\sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{IG}(\alpha_0, \delta_0)$. Conditional on $\sigma^2$ the arms do not talk to each
other, so work on one arm at a time. The exponent of the product of likelihood and prior is
$$
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\left[\sum_{i: D_i = d}(y_i - \mu_d)^2 + \frac{\mu_d^2}{B_0}\right] .
$$
Expand the sum of squares as $n_d\mu_d^2 - 2\mu_d S_d + \sum y_i^2$, with $S_d = \sum_{i:D_i=d} y_i$,
and collect the terms in $\mu_d$:
$$
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\left[\Big(n_d + \tfrac{1}{B_0}\Big)\mu_d^2 - 2\mu_d S_d\right] + \text{const}
= -\frac{n_d + 1/B_0}{2\sigma^2}\left[\mu_d - \frac{S_d}{n_d + 1/B_0}\right]^2 + \text{const} .
$$
Completing the square has done the whole job, so
$$
\mu_d \mid \sigma^2, y \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(b_d, \; \sigma^2 V_d\right), \qquad
V_d = \frac{1}{n_d + 1/B_0}, \qquad b_d = V_d S_d = \frac{n_d}{n_d + 1/B_0}\,\bar y_d .
$$
The posterior mean is the arm mean shrunk towards zero by a factor $n_d/(n_d + 1/B_0)$, which tends to
one as $B_0$ grows or the arm fills up. Because the two arms are conditionally independent, the
difference $\delta = \mu_1 - \mu_0$ has
$$
\delta \mid \sigma^2, y \sim \mathcal{N}\!\big(b_1 - b_0, \; \sigma^2 (V_1 + V_0)\big),
$$
and letting $B_0 \to \infty$ recovers the familiar $\bar y_1 - \bar y_0$ with variance
$\sigma^2(1/n_1 + 1/n_0)$. Integrating $\sigma^2$ out against its inverse-Gamma posterior, whose
parameters update to $\alpha_n = \alpha_0 + n/2$ and
$\delta_n = \delta_0 + \tfrac12\big[\sum_d\sum_{i:D_i=d}(y_i - \bar y_d)^2 + \sum_d n_d \bar
y_d^2/(n_d B_0 + 1)\big]$, turns the Normal into a Student $t$ with $2\alpha_n$ degrees of freedom. In
code it is easier to draw $\sigma^{2(s)}$ first and then $\delta^{(s)}$ given it, which is what the
chunk below does.

Now the part that is easy to get wrong. The parameter $\delta$ is the difference between two population
means. Fisher's sharp null is a different statement altogether: it says $Y_i(1) = Y_i(0)$ for every
single unit $i$, so that treatment changed nothing for anybody. Three consequences follow. First, the
sharp null is not a restriction on $\delta$; it implies $\delta = 0$, but $\delta = 0$ does not imply
it, because individual effects of $+5$ and $-5$ average to zero. Second, under the sharp null every
missing potential outcome is *known* exactly, since $Y_i^{mis} = Y_i$, so the randomisation
distribution of any test statistic can be computed by permuting the treatment labels, with no
likelihood, no prior and no parameter anywhere. Third, and as a result, the two objects answer to
different evidence: a posterior interval for $\delta$ that excludes zero rejects "no average effect" and
says nothing about whether some units were unaffected, while a randomisation test of the sharp null with
a large $p$-value does not argue that the posterior for $\delta$ should be centred at zero. Quote
whichever you computed, and do not translate one into the other.
:::

**Reading the computation.** The event matrix drops any episode too close to the start or end of the sample to supply a full window, so the number of usable episodes can be smaller than the number of dated ones. The posterior is drawn, not sampled by MCMC: the inverse-Gamma draw for the variance comes first and the event-month means are drawn conditional on it.

```{python}
H_LO, H_HI = -12, 24
hs = np.arange(H_LO, H_HI + 1)

def event_matrix(starts, series, h_lo=H_LO, h_hi=H_HI):
    idx = series.index
    rows = []
    for d in starts:
        if d not in idx:
            continue
        i = idx.get_loc(d)
        if i + h_lo < 0 or i + h_hi >= len(idx):
            continue
        rows.append(series.iloc[i + h_lo: i + h_hi + 1].to_numpy())
    return np.array(rows)

abn = mkt - mkt.mean()                  # abnormal = excess return minus its own mean

def event_posterior(E, B0=1.0, alpha_0=3.0, delta_0=3.0 * 0.0018, n_draw=8000, rng=None):
    K, Hn = E.shape
    ybar = E.mean(axis=0)
    B_n = 1.0 / (K + 1.0 / B0)
    m_n = B_n * E.sum(axis=0)
    SSE = ((E - ybar) ** 2).sum() + (K * ybar ** 2 / (K * B0 + 1.0)).sum()
    alpha_n, delta_n = alpha_0 + E.size / 2.0, delta_0 + 0.5 * SSE
    s2 = stats.invgamma(a=alpha_n, scale=delta_n).rvs(n_draw, random_state=rng)
    mu = m_n[None, :] + np.sqrt(s2[:, None] * B_n) * rng.standard_normal((n_draw, Hn))
    return mu, s2

E_base = event_matrix(starts_base, abn)
mu_base, s2_base = event_posterior(E_base, rng=rng_r)
car_base = mu_base[:, hs >= 0].cumsum(axis=1)
print(f"{E_base.shape[0]} usable episodes, {E_base.shape[1]} event months each")
print(f"posterior sd of a monthly abnormal return: {np.sqrt(s2_base.mean()):.4f}")
for h in (0, 5, 11, 23):
    lo, hi = np.quantile(car_base[:, h], [0.05, 0.95])
    print(f"cumulative abnormal return through month {h:>2}: "
          f"mean {car_base[:, h].mean():+.4f} "
          f"90% [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}]  P(<0) = {(car_base[:, h] < 0).mean():.3f}")
```

All twelve baseline episodes supply a full window, so the posterior is built on twelve observations per
event month. The posterior standard deviation of a single monthly abnormal return is $0.0409$, close to
the unconditional $0.0445$ of the raw series, which tells us straight away that lining returns up in
event time has removed very little of their variance. The cumulative abnormal return in the announcement
month itself is $-0.0062$ with a 90 per cent interval of $[-0.0249, +0.0125]$: about six tenths of a
percentage point of underperformance, and an interval four times as wide as the point. By month eleven
the cumulative figure is $-0.0082$ with interval $[-0.0726, +0.0565]$, and the posterior probability
that it is negative is $0.591$, which is barely distinguishable from a coin toss. Only by month
twenty-three does something emerge: $-0.0751$ with interval $[-0.1678, +0.0186]$ and a posterior
probability of $0.908$ that the two-year cumulative abnormal return is negative. Even that is not a
confident finding, and it is the horizon at which one should worry most about other things having
happened in the meantime.

**Reading the computation.** The left panel is the posterior for the mean abnormal return at each event month separately; the right panel accumulates the months from zero onward within each posterior draw, which is why its band widens with the horizon.

```{python}
mu_mean = mu_base.mean(axis=0)
mu_lo, mu_hi = np.quantile(mu_base, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2))
axes[0].fill_between(hs, mu_lo, mu_hi, color="steelblue", alpha=0.3)
axes[0].plot(hs, mu_mean, color="steelblue", lw=1.5)
axes[0].axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=0.8, ls=":")
axes[0].axvline(0, color="firebrick", lw=1.0, ls="--")
axes[0].set(xlabel="months from episode start", ylabel="abnormal monthly return",
            title="Posterior mean abnormal return by event month")
ch = np.arange(0, H_HI + 1)
c_lo, c_hi = np.quantile(car_base, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)
axes[1].fill_between(ch, c_lo, c_hi, color="darkorange", alpha=0.3)
axes[1].plot(ch, car_base.mean(axis=0), color="darkorange", lw=1.5)
axes[1].axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=0.8, ls=":")
axes[1].set(xlabel="months from episode start", ylabel="cumulative abnormal return",
            title="Cumulative abnormal return with 90% band")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The left panel is a reminder of what twelve observations per cell buy. The posterior means jump around
between roughly $-0.03$ and $+0.03$ from one event month to the next, with bands that almost always
straddle zero, and the months before the event look no calmer than the months after it. That last
observation deserves emphasis: if the event genuinely marked a break, we would expect the pre-event
months to be quiet and the post-event months to move, and they are not. The right panel accumulates
those means and shows the slow drift downwards after month twelve, with a band that widens roughly as
the square root of the horizon and never leaves zero behind.

### Nine defensible rules, nine answers

The rule had two free numbers. The next chunk runs the entire exercise over a grid of three thresholds
and three minimum gaps, reporting the posterior for the twelve-month cumulative abnormal return in
each case.

**Reading the computation.** Nothing changes between rows except the two arguments of the dating rule. The model, the prior, the horizon and the data are identical throughout, so every difference across rows is attributable to the definition of the event.

```{python}
rule_rows = []
for thr in (1.0, 1.5, 2.0):
    for quiet in (18, 24, 36):
        st = tightening_starts(fred_r["fed_funds"], 12, thr, quiet)
        Ee = event_matrix(st, abn)
        mu_e, _ = event_posterior(Ee, rng=rng_r)
        car12 = mu_e[:, hs >= 0].cumsum(axis=1)[:, 11]
        lo, hi = np.quantile(car12, [0.05, 0.95])
        rule_rows.append({"threshold": thr, "quiet": quiet, "episodes": Ee.shape[0],
                          "CAR12_mean": car12.mean(), "lo": lo, "hi": hi,
                          "P(<0)": (car12 < 0).mean()})
rules = pd.DataFrame(rule_rows)
print(rules.round(4).to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nspread of posterior means across the nine rules: "
      f"{rules['CAR12_mean'].min():+.4f} to {rules['CAR12_mean'].max():+.4f}")
```

The posterior mean twelve-month cumulative abnormal return runs from $-0.1185$ under the loosest
threshold with the longest gap to $+0.0064$ under the strictest threshold with a twenty-four month gap.
That is a swing of twelve and a half percentage points, and it includes a change of sign. Three of the
nine rules, all of them at the $1.0$ percentage point threshold, produce 90 per cent intervals that
exclude zero, with posterior probabilities of a negative effect of $0.9736$, $0.9695$ and $0.9986$. The
other six do not, and one of them, the $2.0$ point threshold with a twenty-four month gap, puts the
posterior probability of a negative effect at $0.4398$, which is to say slightly below even.

**Reading the computation.** Each row is a complete posterior summary for the same economic question under a different definition of the event. The dotted line is zero.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
lab = [f"{r.threshold:.1f}pp / {int(r.quiet)}m" for r in rules.itertuples()]
ypos = np.arange(len(rules))
ax.errorbar(rules["CAR12_mean"], ypos,
            xerr=[rules["CAR12_mean"] - rules["lo"], rules["hi"] - rules["CAR12_mean"]],
            fmt="o", color="steelblue", capsize=3)
ax.axvline(0.0, color="black", lw=1.0, ls=":")
ax.set_yticks(ypos); ax.set_yticklabels(lab, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("12-month cumulative abnormal return")
ax.set_ylabel("threshold / minimum gap")
ax.set_title("Nine defensible rules, nine different answers")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The figure is the argument. A researcher who reported only the bottom three rows would write that
monetary tightening costs equity investors between six and twelve percentage points over the following
year with high posterior probability. A researcher who reported only the top three would write that the
effect is small and indistinguishable from zero. Both would have used the same data, the same model and
the same prior, and both would have been able to defend their dating rule in a seminar. The posterior
intervals in each row are correct conditional on the rule, and none of them contains any allowance for
the fact that the rule was chosen. This is the reason event studies in macroeconomics are usually
reported over a grid of specifications rather than as a single number, and the reason a Bayesian
treatment of the parameters does not by itself buy any protection: the uncertainty that matters here
lives in a choice the model never sees.

## A synthetic control for restaurants and hotels in 2020

### Estimating the donor weights on the pre-event window

The second exercise has a sharper event. In March 2020 the pandemic closed restaurants and hotels in a
way it did not close software firms or utilities, and the French industry file contains a portfolio,
labelled `meals`, holding exactly those businesses. The synthetic control idea is to build a portfolio
of the other forty-eight industries that tracked `meals` closely before the shock, and then to read the
post-shock difference between the two as the gap left by the event.

Concretely, regress the treated industry's monthly return on the returns of the forty-eight donors over
a pre-event window running from January 2010 to January 2020, with no intercept so that the synthetic
control is a portfolio rather than a portfolio plus a constant. Use the course's conjugate prior,
$w \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 g I_{48})$ and
$\sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{IG}(\alpha_0, \delta_0)$, and note straight away that the classical synthetic
control's restriction to non-negative weights summing to one has been replaced by a Normal prior
centred at zero. That is a substantive change and we shall pay for it in the sensitivity analysis
below. With $121$ pre-event months and $48$ donors the posterior is proper but the design is
uncomfortably close to saturated, which is precisely the situation the derivation after this block is
about.

**Reading the computation.** The posterior is the standard conjugate Normal-inverse-Gamma update with $b_0 = 0$ and $B_0 = gI$. Draws of the weights are taken jointly with the variance so that the gap below inherits the full posterior dependence rather than being evaluated at a point estimate.

```{python}
TREATED = "meals"
pre = ind_r.loc["2010-01":"2020-01"]
post = ind_r.loc["2020-02":"2020-12"]
y_pre, y_post = pre[TREATED].to_numpy(), post[TREATED].to_numpy()
X_pre = pre.drop(columns=[TREATED]).to_numpy()
X_post = post.drop(columns=[TREATED]).to_numpy()
donors = list(pre.drop(columns=[TREATED]).columns)

def donor_posterior(X, y, B0_scale, alpha_0=3.0, delta_0=0.02):
    p_d = X.shape[1]
    B_1 = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(p_d) / B0_scale + X.T @ X)
    b_1 = B_1 @ (X.T @ y)
    alpha_1 = alpha_0 + X.shape[0] / 2.0
    delta_1 = delta_0 + 0.5 * (y @ y - b_1 @ np.linalg.solve(B_1, b_1))
    return b_1, B_1, alpha_1, delta_1

def donor_draws(b_1, B_1, alpha_1, delta_1, n_draw, rng):
    s2 = stats.invgamma(a=alpha_1, scale=delta_1).rvs(n_draw, random_state=rng)
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(B_1)
    return (b_1[None, :] + np.sqrt(s2)[:, None]
            * (rng.standard_normal((n_draw, len(b_1))) @ L.T)), s2

G0 = 4.0
b_1, B_1, a_1, d_1 = donor_posterior(X_pre, y_pre, G0)
w_draws, s2_w = donor_draws(b_1, B_1, a_1, d_1, 8000, rng_r)
fit_pre = X_pre @ b_1
print(f"pre-event window {pre.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {pre.index[-1]:%Y-%m}, "
      f"{X_pre.shape[0]} months, {X_pre.shape[1]} donor industries")
print(f"pre-event fit: R^2 {1 - np.var(y_pre - fit_pre) / np.var(y_pre):.3f}, "
      f"RMSE {np.sqrt(np.mean((y_pre - fit_pre) ** 2)):.4f}, "
      f"residual sd {np.sqrt(s2_w.mean()):.4f}")
print(f"posterior mean weights: sum {b_1.sum():.3f}, "
      f"sum of absolute values {np.abs(b_1).sum():.3f}")
top = np.argsort(-np.abs(b_1))[:8]
print("largest weights: " + ", ".join(f"{donors[j]} {b_1[j]:+.3f}" for j in top))
ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(X_pre.T @ X_pre)
print(f"donor cross-product matrix: smallest eigenvalue {ev.min():.5f}, "
      f"largest {ev.max():.3f}, condition number {ev.max() / ev.min():.0f}")
print(f"prior share of posterior precision at g = {G0}: "
      f"{1 / (1 + G0 * ev.min()):.3f} in the flattest direction, "
      f"{1 / (1 + G0 * ev.max()):.4f} in the stiffest")

synth_post = w_draws @ X_post.T
gap = y_post[None, :] - synth_post
cum_gap = gap.cumsum(axis=1)
for k in range(3):
    print(f"{post.index[k]:%Y-%m}: treated {y_post[k]:+.4f}, "
          f"synthetic control mean {synth_post[:, k].mean():+.4f}")
for k, lbl in [(1, "March 2020"), (2, "February to April 2020"),
               (gap.shape[1] - 1, "February to December 2020")]:
    obj = gap[:, k] if lbl == "March 2020" else cum_gap[:, k]
    lo, hi = np.quantile(obj, [0.05, 0.95])
    print(f"{lbl:<26}: mean {obj.mean():+.4f}  90% [{lo:+.4f}, {hi:+.4f}]  "
          f"P(<0) = {(obj < 0).mean():.3f}")
```

The pre-event fit is decent without being suspiciously good: an $R^2$ of $0.648$ and a root mean squared
error of $0.0207$ per month, against a residual standard deviation of $0.0284$ from the posterior. The
posterior mean weights sum to $0.715$ and their absolute values sum to $1.047$, so the synthetic control
is close to a fully invested long portfolio with a little short exposure, which is what one hopes for
even though nothing in the prior imposed it. The eight largest weights are on soft drinks, rubber and
plastics, clothing, retail, entertainment, transport, beer and toys, a list of consumer-facing and
discretionary industries that is economically sensible for a restaurant and hotel portfolio; the prior
did not know that, and the fact that the data produced it is mild reassurance that the exercise is not
pure numerology.

Now the numbers that matter. In March 2020 the treated industry returned $-0.2212$ while its synthetic
control was expected to return about $-0.094$, leaving a gap with posterior mean $-0.1264$ and a 90 per
cent interval of $[-0.1678, -0.0843]$. The posterior probability that the March gap is negative is
$1.000$ to three decimals, which for a single month of returns is a striking result. Cumulated over
February to April the gap is $-0.0514$ with interval $[-0.1050, +0.0019]$, so already by April most of
the March shortfall had been recovered. Cumulated over the whole eleven months to December 2020 the gap
is $-0.0131$ with interval $[-0.1219, +0.0967]$ and a posterior probability of only $0.578$ that it is
negative. The economics of that sequence is worth stating: restaurants and hotels were hit far harder
than comparable consumer industries in the month the closures began, and then recovered essentially all
of the relative loss over the rest of the year, which is what one would expect of a market pricing a
temporary shock in an industry whose long-run cash flows were largely intact.

**Reading the computation.** The left panel shows monthly returns for the two years around the event so that the March collapse is visible rather than buried in a cumulative level. The right panel is the cumulative gap, and its band comes from the same posterior weight draws.

```{python}
win_idx = pre.index[-13:].append(post.index)
X_win = np.vstack([X_pre[-13:], X_post])
y_win = np.concatenate([y_pre[-13:], y_post])
synth_win = w_draws @ X_win.T
lo_s, hi_s = np.quantile(synth_win, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2))
axes[0].plot(win_idx, y_win, color="firebrick", lw=1.5, label="restaurants and hotels")
axes[0].plot(win_idx, synth_win.mean(axis=0), color="steelblue", lw=1.5,
             label="synthetic control")
axes[0].fill_between(win_idx, lo_s, hi_s, color="steelblue", alpha=0.25)
axes[0].axvline(pd.Timestamp("2020-02-01"), color="black", lw=1.0, ls="--")
axes[0].axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=0.6, ls=":")
axes[0].set(xlabel="date", ylabel="monthly return",
            title="Treated industry and its synthetic control")
axes[0].tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=30, labelsize=8)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
g_lo, g_hi = np.quantile(cum_gap, [0.05, 0.95], axis=0)
axes[1].fill_between(post.index, g_lo, g_hi, color="0.5", alpha=0.35)
axes[1].plot(post.index, cum_gap.mean(axis=0), color="black", lw=1.5)
axes[1].axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=0.8, ls=":")
axes[1].set(xlabel="date", ylabel="cumulative gap",
            title="Cumulative gap with 90% band")
axes[1].tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=30, labelsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

In the left panel the two lines are almost indistinguishable through 2019, which is what the pre-event
$R^2$ of $0.648$ looks like when the common factor is as strong as it is among equity industries. In
February and March 2020 they separate sharply, the treated line falling to $-0.22$ while the synthetic
control falls to about $-0.09$, and then in April the treated line overshoots upward to $+0.19$ against
a synthetic control near $+0.08$. The right panel turns that sequence into the cumulative gap: a sharp
dive to about $-0.16$ by March, a fast partial recovery through April, a second soft patch in the summer
and a return to roughly zero by December, with a band that starts narrow and fans out to about twenty
percentage points wide.

### Why the donor weights are partly a prior statement

The pre-event window has $121$ months and the donor pool has $48$ industries, all of them driven by the
same aggregate equity factor. That combination produces a likelihood that is sharply informative about
a few combinations of the weights and almost silent about many others. The printed diagnostics say how
extreme this is: the donor cross-product matrix has a largest eigenvalue of about $11.5$ and a smallest
of about $0.0089$, a condition number of $1293$. Along the flattest direction the prior supplies $0.966$
of the posterior precision at $g = 4$, and along the stiffest it supplies $0.0213$. The posterior for
the weights is therefore roughly nine hundred and sixty-six parts prior and thirty-four parts data in
one direction, and almost the reverse in another. The derivation below works out the limiting case
exactly, because the limiting case is the clearest way to see what is happening in the approximate one.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation: an identification problem as a flat likelihood, and what the prior does there

Take the linear model $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_n)$, and
suppose two columns are identical, $x_1 = x_2 = x$. Then
$$
X\beta \;=\; \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + (\text{other terms}) \;=\; (\beta_1 + \beta_2)\,x +
(\text{other terms}),
$$
so the fitted values, and therefore the likelihood, depend on $(\beta_1, \beta_2)$ only through the sum.
Change coordinates to $s = \beta_1 + \beta_2$ and $d = \beta_1 - \beta_2$. The log likelihood is
$$
\log L \;=\; -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\big\|y - s\,x - \cdots\big\|^2 + \text{const},
$$
which contains no $d$ at all, so $\partial \log L / \partial d = 0$ everywhere. The likelihood is not
merely weakly informative about $d$; it is exactly constant in that direction, and no amount of data
changes that, because every extra observation adds the same flat term.

Now put the course's prior on it, $\beta \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 g I_2)$ for the two
columns in question. The change of coordinates is linear, $(s,d)^\top = A\beta$ with
$A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$, and $AA^\top = 2I_2$, so the induced prior is
$(s, d)^\top \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 2 g \sigma^2 I_2)$: independent, with $s$ and $d$ each having prior
variance $2g\sigma^2$. Because the prior factorises and the likelihood does not involve $d$, the joint
posterior factorises too,
$$
p(s, d \mid y, \sigma^2) \;\propto\; L(s)\, p(s)\, p(d) \quad \Longrightarrow \quad
p(d \mid y, \sigma^2) \;=\; p(d \mid \sigma^2) \;=\; \mathcal{N}(0, 2g\sigma^2).
$$
The posterior for $d$ is the prior for $d$, exactly and for every sample size. Any credible interval
reported for $\beta_1$ or $\beta_2$ separately is then half a data statement and half a prior statement,
even though the interval for $\beta_1 + \beta_2$ is entirely a data statement. Notice what has and has
not been rescued: the posterior is proper, the sampler converges, the diagnostics are clean, and the
output is still uninformative about the thing that was not identified. A proper prior guarantees a
proper posterior; it guarantees nothing about identification.

The near-collinear case is the same statement with the zero replaced by a small number. Suppose the two
columns are standardised with sample correlation $\rho < 1$, so the two eigenvalues of their
cross-product block are $n(1+\rho)$ and $n(1-\rho)$, the second belonging to the difference direction.
The posterior precision in that direction is $n(1-\rho)/\sigma^2 + 1/(g\sigma^2)$, of which the prior
contributes a share
$$
\frac{1/g}{n(1-\rho) + 1/g} \;=\; \frac{1}{1 + g\,n(1-\rho)} .
$$
With $\rho = 1$ this is one, the exactly flat case. With $n = 121$, $g = 4$ and $\rho = 0.99$ it is
$1/(1 + 4 \times 121 \times 0.01) = 0.171$, so seventeen per cent of what the posterior claims to know
about the difference comes from the prior. Replacing $n(1-\rho)$ by the smallest eigenvalue of the full
$X^\top X$ gives the general version used on the donor pool above, $1/(1 + g\lambda_{\min})$, which the
chunk printed as $0.966$. The practical rule follows: whenever the design has directions the data barely
see, report how the answer moves as $g$ moves, because in those directions moving $g$ is the same thing
as moving the answer.
:::

### Prior sensitivity: how much of the gap is the prior?

The derivation says the prior is doing most of the work in the poorly identified directions of the donor
design. The next chunk makes that concrete by re-running the whole exercise across a grid of prior
scales from $g = 0.01$, which forces the weights almost to zero, up to $g = 20$, which is close to
letting least squares have its way.

**Reading the computation.** Only the prior scale changes across rows. The event, the donors, the window and the treated series are fixed, so any movement in the last three columns is movement caused by the prior alone.

```{python}
g_grid = np.geomspace(0.01, 20.0, 12)
sens = []
for g in g_grid:
    bg, Bg, ag, dg = donor_posterior(X_pre, y_pre, g)
    wd, _ = donor_draws(bg, Bg, ag, dg, 4000, rng_r)
    gp = y_post[None, :] - wd @ X_post.T
    cg = gp.cumsum(axis=1)
    sens.append({"g": g, "sum_abs_w": np.abs(bg).sum(),
                 "pre_RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((y_pre - X_pre @ bg) ** 2)),
                 "mar_mean": gp[:, 1].mean(),
                 "mar_lo": np.quantile(gp[:, 1], 0.05),
                 "mar_hi": np.quantile(gp[:, 1], 0.95),
                 "cum_mean": cg[:, -1].mean(),
                 "cum_lo": np.quantile(cg[:, -1], 0.05),
                 "cum_hi": np.quantile(cg[:, -1], 0.95)})
sens = pd.DataFrame(sens)
print(sens.round(4).to_string(index=False))
```

Read the table from the top. At $g = 0.01$ the absolute weights sum to $0.0592$: the synthetic control
is essentially the zero portfolio, so the "gap" is just the treated industry's own return, and the March
figure is $-0.2104$ with a 90 per cent interval only $0.0169$ wide. That interval is narrow for the
worst possible reason, namely that the prior has fixed the comparison rather than the data. At the other
end, $g = 20$ gives absolute weights summing to $1.8912$, a pre-event root mean squared error of
$0.0189$, and a March gap of $-0.1390$ with an interval $0.1167$ wide, nearly seven times the width at the tight
end. The one-month gap is
reassuringly stable in the middle of the range, moving only between $-0.1259$ and $-0.1407$ for $g$
between $0.3166$ and $20$, so the headline March result is not a prior artefact.

The eleven-month cumulative gap behaves quite differently. It is $+0.1589$ at $g = 0.01$, falls through
$+0.0710$ at $g \approx 0.16$ and $+0.0100$ at $g \approx 1.26$, and turns negative at about
$g \approx 2.5$, reaching $-0.0361$ at $g = 20$. The sign of the answer is a function of the prior. That
is not a bug to be fixed by choosing a prior; it is the correct report, and it says that these data
cannot tell us whether the treated industry ended 2020 above or below its synthetic control.

**Reading the computation.** Both panels plot the same posterior summaries against the prior scale on a log axis, with the dashed vertical line marking the value used for the headline numbers above.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2))
axes[0].fill_between(sens["g"], sens["mar_lo"], sens["mar_hi"],
                     color="firebrick", alpha=0.25)
axes[0].plot(sens["g"], sens["mar_mean"], color="firebrick", lw=1.5)
axes[0].axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=0.8, ls=":")
axes[0].axvline(G0, color="0.4", lw=1.0, ls="--")
axes[0].set_xscale("log")
axes[0].set(xlabel=r"prior scale $g$ on the donor weights", ylabel="March 2020 gap",
            title="One-month gap against the prior")
axes[1].fill_between(sens["g"], sens["cum_lo"], sens["cum_hi"],
                     color="steelblue", alpha=0.25)
axes[1].plot(sens["g"], sens["cum_mean"], color="steelblue", lw=1.5)
axes[1].axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=0.8, ls=":")
axes[1].axvline(G0, color="0.4", lw=1.0, ls="--")
axes[1].set_xscale("log")
axes[1].set(xlabel=r"prior scale $g$ on the donor weights",
            ylabel="eleven-month cumulative gap",
            title="Cumulative gap against the prior")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The two panels are the honest summary of this exercise. On the left the March gap curve is flat over
the entire upper half of the prior range and its band never comes close to zero, so the statement
"restaurants and hotels fell about twelve and a half percentage points more than comparable industries
in March 2020" survives everything we can do to it. On the right the cumulative curve slopes steadily downward
through zero, and its band contains zero over the whole right half of the range, so the statement "the
industry ended the year below its synthetic control" survives nothing. A single reported number from
this exercise would have hidden that difference completely, which is the argument for drawing this
figure every time a shrinkage prior sits on a near-singular design.

## What it would take to call either number causal

Both exercises produced a posterior for a well-defined quantity, and in both cases that quantity is a
gap between an observed path and a constructed comparison. Turning a gap into a causal effect requires
assumptions that the data cannot supply, and it is worth naming them against the numbers we have.

Parallel trends is the first. For the synthetic control the assumption needed is that, absent the
pandemic, the treated industry's return would have continued to equal the synthetic control's return up
to mean-zero noise. The pre-event fit gives some evidence about this, and an $R^2$ of $0.648$ with a
monthly residual standard deviation of $0.0284$ is the relevant number: the comparison was good to about
two point eight percentage points a month before the event, which is already more than a fifth of the
March gap of $0.1264$ in a single month, and it is more than the entire eleven-month cumulative gap of $0.0131$.
So the March number survives a parallel-trends worry comfortably and the annual number does not survive
it at all. For the event study the corresponding assumption is that the abnormal return would have been
zero in the absence of tightening, and the left panel of the event-time figure argued against exactly
that, because the pre-event months are as noisy as the post-event ones.

No anticipation is the second, and it is where the event study is weakest. The federal funds rate is set
by a committee whose intentions are discussed publicly for months in advance, and the rule we used dates
the episode from the moment a twelve-month change crossed a threshold, which is by construction long
after the first move. If markets priced the cycle before our date, the effect has already happened
before event month zero and the posterior we computed is looking in the wrong place. The synthetic
control does better here, since the closures of March 2020 were not anticipated a year in advance,
though the market clearly began repricing in late February, which is why we started the post window at
February rather than March.

No interference, or the stable unit treatment value assumption, is the third and in both exercises it is
the most obviously violated. The synthetic control's donors are other equity portfolios in the same
economy during the same pandemic: airlines, clothing retailers and entertainment firms were all hit by
the closures, so the control group is treated too. The direction of that bias is towards zero, meaning
that a true effect of the pandemic on restaurants and hotels relative to a genuinely untreated
comparison would be larger than the $-0.1264$ we report. In the event study, interference is worse
still, since the whole market is a single unit and a tightening cycle affects the comparison implicit
in the sample mean we subtracted.

Add to all of this the fact that neither the treatment nor the event date was assigned by anyone, and
the conclusion is the one this section began with. What we have computed are posteriors for descriptive
gaps that are correctly propagated through the model and the prior. They are not estimates of causal
effects, and the way to make them into estimates of causal effects is not a better sampler or a wider
prior but a research design these files do not contain.

## Takeaways

A causal question is a missing-data question, and writing the finite-sample estimand as
$n^{-1}\sum_i(2D_i-1)(Y_i - Y_i^{mis})$ makes that explicit: the Bayesian answer imputes the missing arm
from the fitted opposite-arm predictive, so consistency, unconfoundedness and overlap are the things
doing the identifying and the posterior is doing the accounting. The difference-in-means posterior
follows from completing one square and shrinks each arm mean by $n_d/(n_d + 1/B_0)$, but it is a
statement about $\delta = \mu_1 - \mu_0$ and not about Fisher's sharp null, which is a claim about every
unit and is tested by permutation rather than by a prior. When the design has a direction the likelihood
cannot see, the posterior in that direction is the prior, exactly, however clean the diagnostics look,
and the near-collinear version of that statement puts the prior's share of the posterior precision at
$1/(1 + g\lambda_{\min})$, which on the donor design of this chapter is $0.966$. The two real-data
exercises then show what that costs in practice: a mechanical dating rule for Federal Reserve tightening
moves the twelve-month cumulative abnormal return from $-0.1185$ to $+0.0064$ across nine equally
defensible specifications, and a synthetic control for restaurants and hotels gives a March 2020 gap of
$-0.1264$ that is stable across the upper half of the prior range alongside an eleven-month
cumulative gap of $-0.0131$ whose very sign is chosen by the prior. Report the specification grid and
the prior sweep, and call the result a descriptive gap until parallel trends, no anticipation and no
interference have been argued rather than assumed.


## Reading guide and sources

Greenberg (2008), Sections 11.1–11.2, for treatment models and endogenous covariates. Hill (2011) and Chipman et al. (2010) supply the BART application; UPM supplies the conditional-update mechanics, not a BART implementation.

The explanations and exercises are adapted to this course's notation and weekly
structure; consult the cited originals for the full treatments.
